College Radio Submissions for Independent Artists

College radio remains one of the more approachable parts of the radio ecosystem for independent musicians, but the process is rarely as simple as sending the same email to every station. Different stations have different formats, schedules, submission rules, and decision-makers. A useful campaign starts by identifying stations that actually make sense for your music.

Who should you contact at a college radio station?

Look first for a music director, genre director, program director, specialty-show host, or a clearly identified music-submission address. A general station inbox can still be useful when no individual contact is published, but a relevant human contact is usually better than sending blindly.

Titles vary from station to station. Some student-run stations divide responsibility by genre. Others have one music director handling most incoming releases. Read the station's own website before assuming who makes programming decisions.

How should you submit music to college radio?

Follow the station's stated submission process first. If it accepts digital submissions, send a concise message identifying the artist, genre, release, relevant location or story, and a streaming link. Avoid enormous attachments unless the station specifically asks for them.

The strongest outreach usually explains why the release belongs at that particular station. Mentioning a relevant specialty show, regional connection, or programming fit is more useful than claiming that a track is simply “perfect for radio.”

Do college radio stations accept independent music?

Many do, although policies vary widely. College and noncommercial stations often have more programming flexibility than large commercial stations, and specialty programs may actively seek music outside major-label pipelines. That does not mean every station accepts unsolicited music or that submission guarantees airplay.

Treat the station's published rules as authoritative. Radio promotion works better as targeted research than as mass email.

Where a radio contact list helps

The slow part of outreach is often not writing the pitch. It is finding the stations, identifying the relevant people, organizing the information, and keeping track of whom you have contacted.

RadioReach is built around that research problem. The Radio Reach Vault provides organized radio station contact information so independent artists can spend less time assembling a prospect list and more time deciding which stations are actually worth approaching.
